lessons.title: Tools for irrigation maintenance
lessons.html:
Irrigation on the farm

Irrigation gives crops water when there is not enough rain. On South African farms you may see drip lines in orchards and vineyards, sprinklers in vegetable lands, and big centre pivots in maize or lucerne fields. Water comes from a dam, river, borehole or canal, through a pump, filters and pipes, to the plants.

Main parts of a system

  • Pump: pushes the water.
  • Filter: catches sand and dirt so drippers and sprinklers do not block.
  • Main line and sub-mains: the big pipes.
  • Valves: open and close water to each block.
  • Laterals: small pipes or drip lines along the rows.
  • Emitters: drippers, micro-sprinklers or sprinklers.

Tools you need

ToolUse
SpadeDig to find and fix buried pipes
Pipe cutter or sharp knifeCut pipe cleanly
Joiners, end plugs, goof plugsJoin pipes and close holes
Hole punchMake holes for new drippers
Spare drippers and sprinkler nozzlesReplace broken ones
Spanners and pliersOpen filters and fittings
Brush and bucketClean filters
Hose clampsHold joins tight

Getting the tools

  • Ask your supervisor what job you will do.
  • Collect the right tools and spare parts from the store. Sign for them if the farm asks.
  • Check the tools: sharp knife, no broken handles.
  • Put small parts in a bag or bucket so you do not lose them.
  • After work, clean tools and return them.

Safety

  • Cut away from your body with the knife.
  • Never touch electric pumps or switch boxes. Only trained people work on them.
  • Be careful near dams and canals. Do not swim in them.
  • Wear boots; wet soil is slippery.

lessons.title: Running the irrigation system
lessons.html:
Follow the set procedure

Every farm has its own procedure for irrigation. Your supervisor tells you which block to water and for how long. Follow the steps exactly.

Before you start

  1. Check that the right valves are open for the block you must water, and others are closed.
  2. Check the filter is clean.
  3. Walk the line and look for broken pipes.

Starting

  1. The pump is started by a trained person, or by you if you have been shown how.
  2. Open valves slowly. Opening fast causes a water hammer that can burst pipes.
  3. Check the pressure gauge if there is one. Tell your supervisor if it is too high or too low.

While it runs

  • Walk the rows. Look for leaks, burst pipes, and drippers or sprinklers that do not work.
  • Look for water running off the land or making pools. This wastes water.
  • Fix small leaks with a joiner or goof plug. Report big problems.
  • Write down the start time.

Stopping

  1. At the right time, close the valves slowly, or ask for the pump to be stopped.
  2. Write down the stop time and any problems.

Simple maintenance

  • Clean filters often: open, wash the screen or discs with clean water and a brush, and close tightly.
  • Flush lines: open the end of drip lines to let dirty water out, then close them.
  • Clean blocked drippers or replace them.
  • Repair cuts in pipes with joiners.
  • Keep weeds and soil away from sprinklers.

Animals, rats, tractors and spades often damage pipes. Check after work in the lands.

lessons.title: How water affects crop growth
lessons.html:
Why plants need water

Plants take up water through their roots. Water carries food from the soil into the plant and keeps leaves cool. Without enough water a plant wilts, grows slowly and gives a small crop.

Too little water

  • Leaves hang down (wilt), curl or turn yellow.
  • Fruit and grain stay small.
  • Plants may die in hot weather.

Too much water

  • Soil gets waterlogged; roots cannot breathe and may rot.
  • Fertiliser is washed away below the roots.
  • Diseases grow more easily.
  • Water and electricity are wasted, and that costs the farm money.

Things that change how much water a crop needs

  • Weather: hot, windy days dry the soil fast. Cool, cloudy days need less water. Rain means less irrigation.
  • Soil: sandy soil drains fast and needs water more often. Clay soil holds water longer.
  • Crop and its age: young plants have small roots and need small, regular amounts. Big plants with fruit need more.
  • Time of day: sprinkler watering in the heat and wind loses water to the air.

Checking the soil

You can check soil moisture by digging a small hole near the roots and squeezing the soil. If it falls apart like dust, it is dry. If it holds together and feels damp, it is fine. If water drips out, it is too wet. Some farms use probes or tensiometers; your supervisor reads them.

Water is precious in South Africa. Farms need permission to take water, and every drop wasted is money lost. Report waste when you see it.

Key points

  • Collect the right tools and parts, and return them clean.
  • Open and close valves slowly.
  • Walk the lines and fix or report leaks.
  • Clean filters and flush lines regularly.
  • Too little or too much water both harm crops.
